subject_entity.notes: Athenagoras's philosophical defense of bodily resurrection c. 177.

object_entity.notes: Athenian Christian philosopher who addressed an embassy to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus c. 177 defending Christians and articulating Logos theology.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Arguments defending the truth of resurrection must precede all inquiry about it; God who created what did not exist can certainly restore what has been dissolved; disbelief in resurrection has no reasonable foundation.

subject_entity.notes: Tertullian's treatise on prayer c. 198-200; earliest known systematic exposition of the Lord's Prayer; includes eucharistic and fasting references.

object_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Tertullian opens with the statement that the Spirit of God, the Word of God, the Reason of God — the Word of Reason, the Reason and Spirit of the Word — Jesus Christ our Lord, determined a new form of prayer for the new disciples of the new covenant.
passage.notes: Lord's Prayer as new form of prayer given by Christ; earliest systematic commentary on the Our Father

subject_entity.notes: Hippolytus set himself up as rival bishop of Rome c. 217 after the election of Callistus I, whom he accused of modalism and moral laxity; sometimes called the first antipope; the schism persisted through the pontificates of Urban I and Pontian until reconciliation in Sardinian exile c. 235.

evidence.notes: Hippolytus Ref. 9.11-12 describes the schism with Callistus c. 217 CE; year inferred from context.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Callistus alleged that the parable of the tares growing together with the wheat was spoken in reference to the Church: sinners should remain in the Church. He also affirmed that the ark of Noah was a figure of the Church, in which were dogs, hawks, and other unclean animals — so must the Church tolerate sinners.
passage.notes: Callistus defends leniency toward sinners using parables of tares and Noah's ark; penitential controversy

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Callistus, having been appointed over the cemetery by Zephyrinus, brought many into his following. He was the first to invent the device of conniving at the sensual pleasures of men, saying that all men had their sins forgiven by himself. For he even permitted women of rank, if they were unmarried and burned with lust, to have a companion of the rank of slave or freedman.
passage.notes: Hippolytus attacks Callistus for moral laxity; permitting marriages between social classes; forgiving grave sins
